$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The displayed sign in $Y$ fixes all later orientation and rotation conventions.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

derivations.claim: Multiplying the entries of the matrices in [F1] gives the nine row-by-column products $X^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I$, $XY=\begin{pmatrix}i&0\\0&-i\end{pmatrix}=iZ$, $XZ=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=-iY$, $YX=\begin{pmatrix}-i&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix}=-iZ$, $Y^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I$, $YZ=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}=iX$, $ZX=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=iY$, $ZY=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix}=-iX$, and $Z^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=I$.

By [F1] and [F2], $X^*=X$, $Y^*=Y$, and $Z^*=Z$; the diagonal entries of each product $X^*X,Y^*Y,Z^*Z$ are $1$ and its off-diagonal entries are $0$, so each product is $I$. By [F4] each is a unitary operator, in the sense of [F5].

The six off-diagonal products in step 1.1 have opposite signs when their order is reversed, so the matrices anticommute pairwise and the table is exactly the $\delta,\epsilon$ product formula in the Statement. The same matrices have $\operatorname{tr}(X)=\operatorname{tr}(Y)=\operatorname{tr}(Z)=0$ and $\operatorname{tr}(I)=2$ by [F3]. Taking traces in step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise.

The **qubit space** is the one-qubit register $Q_2=\mathbb C^2$ of [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]], with ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)=(e_0,e_1)$. This basis is orthonormal by [[thm-qc-computational-basis-orthonormal]]. A **qubit state** is a density operator on $Q_2$ in the sense of [[def-qc-density-operator]], namely a non-negative endomorphism of trace one. A **pure qubit state** is a pure-state ray on $Q_2$ in the sense of [[def-qc-pure-state-and-ray]]. The Bloch coordinates and their state-space constraints are defined and proved in the following items on this page.

The term qubit here names the two-dimensional register and its mathematical state space. No physical preparation or measurement postulate is part of this definition.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The displayed sign in $Y$ fixes all later orientation and rotation conventions.

For the matrices $X,Y,Z$ of [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]], each is self-adjoint and unitary, and $X^2=Y^2=Z^2=I$. Distinct Pauli matrices anticommute. For $j,k\in\{x,y,z\}$,
$$\sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}I+i\sum_{\ell\in\{x,y,z\}}\epsilon_{jk\ell}\sigma_\ell,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}.$$
Here $\sigma_x=X,\sigma_y=Y,\sigma_z=Z$, $\delta_{jk}=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\epsilon$ is the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{xyz}=1$. Also $\operatorname{tr}(I)=2$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_j)=0$.

Let $Q_2$ be the qubit space of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $Q_2$ in the sense of [[def-qc-density-operator]]. Define its candidate Bloch coordinates in $\mathbb C^3$ by
$$r_j(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_j)\quad(j\in\{x,y,z\}),\qquad \mathbf r(\rho):=(r_x(\rho),r_y(\rho),r_z(\rho)).$$
For any $\mathbf r=(r_x,r_y,r_z)\in\mathbb R^3$, define the associated Hermitian-matrix candidate
$$\rho(\mathbf r):=\frac12\bigl(I+r_xX+r_yY+r_zZ\bigr).$$
Write $\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}:=r_xX+r_yY+r_zZ$ and
$$\|\mathbf r\|_2:=\sqrt{r_x^2+r_y^2+r_z^2}.$$
The next theorem proves that these trace coordinates are real and that every Hermitian trace-one $2\times2$ matrix is uniquely $\rho(\mathbf r)$; the positivity theorem determines which real-coordinate candidates are states.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: For arbitrary real $\mathbf r$, the matrices in [F6] give $\rho(\mathbf r)=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+r_z&r_x-ir_y\\r_x+ir_y&1-r_z\end{pmatrix}$. Its diagonal entries are real, its lower-left entry is the conjugate of the upper-right, and its trace is $1$, so it is Hermitian trace one.

Write the arbitrary Hermitian trace-one matrix $\rho=\begin{pmatrix}a&z\\\overline z&1-a\end{pmatrix}$ with $a\in\mathbb R$: [F2] makes the computational basis orthonormal, and [F3]–[F4] give the conjugate-transpose matrix criterion for $\rho^*=\rho$, so its diagonal entries are real and its lower-left entry is the conjugate of the upper-right; trace one fixes the second diagonal entry. Put $r_x=2\operatorname{Re}z$, $r_y=-2\operatorname{Im}z$, and $r_z=2a-1$, which are real. The matrices in [F6] and formula in [F8] give $\rho(\mathbf r)=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1+r_z&r_x-ir_y\\r_x+ir_y&1-r_z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a&z\\\overline z&1-a\end{pmatrix}=\rho$. This proves existence.

For the entries $a,z$ of step 1.2, direct multiplication using [F6] and summing diagonal entries by [F9] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho X)=z+\overline z=2\operatorname{Re}z=r_x$, $\operatorname{tr}(\rho Y)=i(z-\overline z)=-2\operatorname{Im}z=r_y$, and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho Z)=a-(1-a)=2a-1=r_z$. If $\rho=\rho(\mathbf s)$ for another real vector $\mathbf s$, [F7] applied to [F8] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_j)=s_j$ for each $j$, so $\mathbf s=\mathbf r$ and uniqueness follows. When $\rho$ is a density operator, [F5] makes it Hermitian and trace one, and [F8] identifies these same real trace coordinates with the map $\mathbf r(\rho)$.

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

Let $Q_2$ be the qubit space of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $Q_2$ in the sense of [[def-qc-density-operator]]. Define its candidate Bloch coordinates in $\mathbb C^3$ by
$$r_j(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho\sigma_j)\quad(j\in\{x,y,z\}),\qquad \mathbf r(\rho):=(r_x(\rho),r_y(\rho),r_z(\rho)).$$
For any $\mathbf r=(r_x,r_y,r_z)\in\mathbb R^3$, define the associated Hermitian-matrix candidate
$$\rho(\mathbf r):=\frac12\bigl(I+r_xX+r_yY+r_zZ\bigr).$$
Write $\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}:=r_xX+r_yY+r_zZ$ and
$$\|\mathbf r\|_2:=\sqrt{r_x^2+r_y^2+r_z^2}.$$
The next theorem proves that these trace coordinates are real and that every Hermitian trace-one $2\times2$ matrix is uniquely $\rho(\mathbf r)$; the positivity theorem determines which real-coordinate candidates are states.

For every $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$, the matrix $\rho(\mathbf r)$ of [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]] is Hermitian with trace one. Conversely, every Hermitian trace-one matrix $\rho\in M_2(\mathbb C)$ has a unique vector $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$ such that
$$\rho=\rho(\mathbf r)=\frac12\bigl(I+r_xX+r_yY+r_zZ\bigr).$$
For a qubit density operator this vector is exactly $(\operatorname{tr}(\rho X),\operatorname{tr}(\rho Y),\operatorname{tr}(\rho Z))$, the coordinate map of [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. In particular all three trace coordinates of every density operator are real.

If $\rho$ is a qubit density operator and $\mathbf r$ is its unique Bloch vector, then
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=\frac{1+\|\mathbf r\|_2^2}{2}.$$
The state $\rho$ is pure, meaning it is the projector of a pure-state ray, if and only if $\|\mathbf r\|_2=1$.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product $H$, the map sending a ray $[u]$ to the rank-one projector $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ of any unit representative is well-defined and bijective onto the rank-one orthogonal projections on $H$. Each $P_u$ is non-negative and has trace one.
